searchText: > <@!375471494081282048> I think the fee burning may be treated as taxes and the economical models usually say that introduction of taxes is being split between miners and users in a ratio dependent on the price elasticity. <@!273808422753796097> was calculating the elasticity to be around 2 recently so I think we can exactly calculate the percentage of the tax that will be absorbed by the miners (should be 60% or so of the top of my head?) this isn't quite correct Because it's not a new tax being introduced, it's an existing regulatory mechanism (the quantity limit) being replaced by a new regulatory mechanism (the floating fee) so the outcome should be that average fees stay about the same but instead of the fee going to miners a large part of it gets burned at more-than-very-short timescales, the supply curve is still a vertical line at 10 million, so the gasprice that users pay will still be the intersection of that vertical line with their demand curve ie. unchanged from before <@!273808422753796097> Is the x2 block elasticity required to preserve the benefits of EIP-1559 Would it work with something less, x1.5 for example ? We talked with Geth team and they are really concerned about the x2 multiplier, saying that the system already operates at its limit. x1.5 would allow 33% attacks > x1.5 would allow 33% attacks <@!273808422753796097> Could you explain briefly how ? The lower the elasticity, the less hash power is required to drive the base fee down. Basically you only need 34% to mine empty blocks to make the average block size below the target It doesn't break things entirely, it is still non-profitable to mine empty blocks. However, the larger the elasticity, the harder it is (more hashing power required to collude) to force the base fee down by mining empty blocks. If you go down to 1x elasticity, it takes 0 hash power to mine enough empty blocks to drive the base fee to 0. 😉 Ok thanks <@!273808422753796097> and <@!301186049323958275>

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: > <@!375471494081282048> I think the fee burning may be treated as taxes and the economical models usually say that introduction of taxes is being split between miners and users in a ratio dependent on the price elasticity. <@!273808422753796097> was calculating the elasticity to be around 2 recently so I think we can exactly calculate the percentage of the tax that will be absorbed by the miners (should be 60% or so of the top of my head?)

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Because it's not a new tax being introduced, it's an existing regulatory mechanism (the quantity limit) being replaced by a new regulatory mechanism (the floating fee)

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: so the outcome should be that average fees stay about the same but instead of the fee going to miners a large part of it gets burned

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: at more-than-very-short timescales, the supply curve is still a vertical line at 10 million, so the gasprice that users pay will still be the intersection of that vertical line with their demand curve

excerpts.author: abdel.stark
excerpts.content: <@!273808422753796097> Is the x2 block elasticity required to preserve the benefits of EIP-1559 Would it work with something less, x1.5 for example ? We talked with Geth team and they are really concerned about the x2 multiplier, saying that the system already operates at its limit.

excerpts.author: abdel.stark
excerpts.content:
> x1.5 would allow 33% attacks
<@!273808422753796097> Could you explain briefly how ?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: The lower the elasticity, the less hash power is required to drive the base fee down.

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Basically you only need 34% to mine empty blocks to make the average block size below the target

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: It doesn't break things entirely, it is still non-profitable to mine empty blocks.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: However, the larger the elasticity, the harder it is (more hashing power required to collude) to force the base fee down by mining empty blocks.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: If you go down to 1x elasticity, it takes 0 hash power to mine enough empty blocks to drive the base fee to 0.  😉
